# Introduction


# Naive set theory

We begin with two primitive informal notions: **objects** and **sets**.
Roughly speaking, a set is a collection of objects, and the most basic question we can ask is whether a given object belongs to a given set.
If the object $x$ belongs to the set $A$, we write
$$
x\in A,
$$
and if it does not belong to $A$, we write
$$
x\notin A.
$$

An intuitive example of set is given by the set of natural numbers
$$
\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,3,\dots\},
$$
which, at this stage, should be understood only informally.

::: {.callout-warning title="Numbers will NOT be built"}

::: {#rem-numbers-treated-informally}

In this course, we will unfortunately **not** build the set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$, of integers $\mathbb{Z}$, of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, or of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ from scratch.

Doing so carefully would be supremely satisfying from the intellectual point of view, but it would also require a substantial amount of additional time to go through a similarly substantial amount of foundational material.

In any case, we will explicitly point out the properties and subtleties of these number systems whenever they become relevant.

:::

:::

This informal viewpoint is useful, but also delicate.
If one tries to take the notion of set completely literally and declare that every possible collection of objects is automatically a set, contradictions appear.
The most famous one is [**Russell's paradox**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell%27s_paradox), which can be explained through the [**barber's paradox**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barber_paradox): imagine a barber who lives in a village and shaves exactly those people in the village who do not shave themselves.
Does the barber shave himself?
If he does, then by definition he should not; if he does not, then by definition he should.
The set-theoretic Russel's paradox has the same logical flavour and warns us that foundations must be handled with care.
Taking that issue seriously would force us into a long discussion on logic and the foundations of mathematics, which is far beyond the scope of this course.
So we adopt a pragmatic axiomatic point of view.

In these notes, we work with **objects** and **sets**, and we regard every set as an object.
However, not every object is automatically considered to be a set.
For instance, the number [$42$](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/for-math-fans-a-hitchhikers-guide-to-the-number-42/) is an object, but [Axiom 4](#axm-axioms-set-theory) below assures there is  set $\{42\}$ containing the number 42, which is also an object.






::: {.callout-note title="Axioms of Set Theory"}

::: {#axm-axioms-set-theory}

1) **Sets Are Objects**: Every set is an object.

2) **Equality of Sets**: Two sets $A$ and $B$ are said to be **equal** if they have exactly the same elements, that is, if for every object $x$ one has
$$
x\in A \Longleftrightarrow x\in B.
$$
Thus, when dealing with sets, what matters is not the order in which the elements are written, nor how many times they are listed, but only which objects belong to the set.

3) **Empty Set**: There exists a set with no elements, called the **empty set** and denoted by
$$
\emptyset=\{\}.
$$

4) **Singleton sets and pair sets**: If $x$ is an object, then there exists a set whose only element is $x$.
This set is called the **singleton** associated with $x$ and is denoted by
$$
\{x\}.
$$
If $x$ and $y$ are objects, then there exists a set whose elements are exactly $x$ and $y$.
This set is denoted by
$$
\{x,y\}.
$$
If $x=y$, this is just the singleton $\{x\}$.

5) **Pairwise Union**: If $A$ and $B$ are sets, then there exists a set whose elements are precisely those objects that belong to $A$ or to $B$.
This set is called the **union** of $A$ and $B$ and is denoted by
$$
A\cup B.
$$

6) **Specification**: Let $A$ be a set, and let $P(x)$ be a property referring to objects $x$.
Then there exists a set consisting of exactly those elements of $A$ for which $P(x)$ is true.
We denote it by
$$
\{x\in A \,:\, P(x)\}.
$$
This is the basic operation that allows us to carve out subsets from sets that already exist.

7) **Replacement**: Let $A$ be a set, and suppose that to each element $x\in A$ we assign a unique object $f(x)$.
Then the collection of all such outputs
$$
\{f(x)\,:\, x\in A\}
$$
is again a set.
This axiom says that if we start with a set and systematically replace each of its elements by another object, the resulting collection is still a set.

8) **Natural Numbers**: There exists a set $\mathbb{N}$ whose elements are called the **natural numbers**, together with a distinguished element $0\in\mathbb{N}$ and a successor operation
$$
n\mapsto n+1
$$
which sends each natural number to another natural number.

We will not discuss the formal [Peano axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peano_axioms) here, nor will we attempt to construct the integers, rationals, or reals from $\mathbb{N}$.
Instead, we use the familiar intuitive number systems and record explicitly whatever algebraic or order-theoretic properties we need later on.

:::

:::

The previous axioms are enough for the level of set theory we need in this course.


::: {.callout-note title="Subset"}

::: {#def-subset}

Given two sets $A$ and $X$, we write
$$
A\subseteq X
$$
if every element of $A$ is also an element of $X$.
In this case, we call $A$ a **subset** of $X$. 

If $A\neq X$, which means there is at least one element of $X$ that is not in $A$, we say $A$ is a **strict subset**, and write $A\subset X$.

:::

:::


::: {.callout-note title="Intersection"}

::: {#def-intersection}

If $A$ and $B$ are subsets of $X$, we define their **intersection** is the set
$$
A\cap B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\in B\}.
$$
:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Difference and complement set"}

::: {#def-difference-complement}

If $A$ and $B$ are subsets of $X$, their **difference**  is the set
$$
A\setminus B:=\{x\in A \,:\, x\notin B\}.
$$

In particular, when $A=X$, the difference $X\setminus B$  is called the **complement** of $B$ in $X$, and it is often denoted as $B^{c}$ when $X$ is understood from the context.

:::

:::


::: {.callout-note title="Cartesian product"}

::: {#def-cartesian-product}

For two sets $A$ and $B$, their **Cartesian product** is the set
$$
A\times B:=\{(a,b)\,:\, a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
$$
Here $(a,b)$ denotes the ordered pair formed by $a$ and $b$.

More generally, if $A_{1},\dots,A_{n}$ are sets, we define their **finite Cartesian product** by
$$
\prod_{j=1}^{n}A_{j}
:=
\left\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\,:\, x_{j}\in A_{j}\ \mbox{ for every } j=1,\dots,n\right\}.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Ordered pairs"}

::: {#rem-ordered-pairs}

In order for @def-cartesian-product to actually make sense, we must be able to consider $(a,b)$ an object, and to be sure that $(a,b)$ is the same object as $(a',b')$ if and only if $a=a'$ and $b=b'$. 



To do this, we need the so-called [Kuratowski's definition of ordered pairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_pair#Kuratowski's_definition), which defines
$$
(a,b):=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}.
$$


:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Relation on a set"}

::: {#def-relation}

Let $X$ be a set.
A **relation** on $X$ is a subset
$$
R\subseteq X\times X.
$$
If $(x,y)\in R$, we often write
$$
x\,R\,y.
$$

Thus, a relation is simply a systematic way of declaring, for some ordered pairs $(x,y)$ of elements of $X$, that $x$ is related to $y$.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Order relations"}

::: {#def-order-relations}

Let $X$ be a set, and let $\leq$ be a relation on $X$.
We say that $\leq$ is a **partial order** if the following properties hold for every $x,y,z\in X$:

1. **Reflexivity**: $x\leq x$.
2. **Antisymmetry**: if $x\leq y$ and $y\leq x$, then $x=y$.
3. **Transitivity**: if $x\leq y$ and $y\leq z$, then $x\leq z$.

If, in addition, for every $x,y\in X$ one has either $x\leq y$ or $y\leq x$, then $\leq$ is called a **total order** or **linear order**.

When the order is total, we also write
$$
x<y
$$
to mean that $x\leq y$ and $x\neq y$.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Upper and lower bounds"}

::: {#def-upper-lower-bounds}

Let $X$ be a totally ordered set, and let $A\subseteq X$.

An element $u\in X$ is called an **upper bound** for $A$ if
$$
a\leq u
$$
for every $a\in A$.

An element $\ell\in X$ is called a **lower bound** for $A$ if
$$
\ell\leq a
$$
for every $a\in A$.

An upper bound $s$ for $A$ is called the **least upper bound** or **supremum** of $A$ if
$$
s\leq u
$$
for every upper bound $u$ of $A$.

A lower bound $m$ for $A$ is called the **greatest lower bound** or **infimum** of $A$ if
$$
\ell\leq m
$$
for every lower bound $\ell$ of $A$.

If $A$ has a least upper bound, we write
$$
\sup A.
$$
If $A$ has a greatest lower bound, we write
$$
\inf A.
$$

A totally ordered set is said to have the **least-upper-bound property** if every nonempty subset which is bounded above has a supremum.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Field"}

::: {#def-field}

A **field** is a set $F$ endowed with two operations, called **addition** and **multiplication**, together with two distinguished elements $0,1\in F$ with $0\neq 1$, such that the following hold for every $x,y,z\in F$:

1. **Associativity of addition and multiplication**:
$$
(x+y)+z=x+(y+z),\qquad (xy)z=x(yz).
$$

2. **Commutativity of addition and multiplication**:
$$
x+y=y+x,\qquad xy=yx.
$$

3. **Neutral elements**:
$$
x+0=x,\qquad x\cdot 1=x.
$$

4. **Additive inverses**: for every $x\in F$, there exists an element $-x\in F$ such that
$$
x+(-x)=0.
$$

5. **Multiplicative inverses**: for every $x\in F$ with $x\neq 0$, there exists an element $x^{-1}\in F$ such that
$$
x\,x^{-1}=1.
$$

6. **Distributive law**:
$$
x(y+z)=xy+xz.
$$

These axioms allow us to perform the usual algebraic manipulations with sums, differences, products, and quotients by nonzero elements.
The familiar number systems $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are examples of fields.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Ordered field"}

::: {#def-ordered-field}

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ in the sense of @def-field, together with a total order $\leq$ (with associated strict order $<$), such that

1. if $x<y$, then
$$
x+z<y+z
$$
for every $z\in F$;
2. if $0<x$ and $0<y$, then
$$
0<xy.
$$

Thus, an ordered field is a field in which the algebraic operations and the order relation are compatible.
The rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ are the standard examples.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Characterization of the real numbers"}

::: {#thm-characterization-reals}

There exists, up to order-preserving field isomorphism, only one ordered field with the least-upper-bound property.
That ordered field is what mathematicians call the set of **real numbers**, and it can be proved to "coincide" with the intuitive idea we already have of $\mathbb{R}$.

We will not prove this theorem here.
Instead, we simply accept that the familiar real numbers form an ordered field with the least-upper-bound property and use that fact throughout the course.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="The standard number sets inside $\mathbb{R}$"}

::: {#def-standard-number-sets}

Once $\mathbb{R}$ is in place, we regard the standard number systems as nested subsets
$$
\mathbb{N}\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\subseteq \mathbb{Q}\subseteq \mathbb{R}.
$$
Here $\mathbb{N}$ denotes the natural numbers, $\mathbb{Z}$ the integers, $\mathbb{Q}$ the rational numbers, and $\mathbb{R}$ the real numbers.

We will use these inclusions in the usual informal way and think of the algebraic operations and the order on the smaller number sets as inherited from $\mathbb{R}$.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Induction principle"}

::: {#prp-induction-principle}

Let $P(n)$ be a statement depending on a natural number $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
Assume that

1. $P(0)$ is true;
2. whenever $P(n)$ is true, then $P(n+1)$ is also true.

Then $P(n)$ is true for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

This is the **principle of mathematical induction**.
In practice, it allows us to prove infinitely many statements, one for each natural number, by verifying only a base case and one inductive step.

:::

:::

# Functions



::: {.callout-warning title="How we will write functions"}

::: {#rem-how-we-write-functions}

Sometimes, we may be forced to talk about the function $f\colon D\subseteq X\rightarrow Y$ given by $f(x)=y$ multiple times when proving a theorem, solving an exercise, or discussing an idea.
To avoid an absurd amount of notationally-heavy repetitions, once the domain, the input space, the output  space, and the explicit rule $f(x)=y$ have been clearly defined as above, we will often write just $f(x)=y$, or even just $f$, for the rest of the proof of the theorem, or of the exercise, or of the discussion.

Moreover, sometimes we may be introducing a subset $D\subseteq X$, and later introduce a function having $D$ as domain. 
In this case, we often writes $f\colon D\rightarrow Y$ given by $f(x)=y$ omitting the input space since it is clear from the context.

:::

:::

# Real numbers

We need to introduce various types of intervals. These objects help in formalizing the way $x$ approaches $x_{0}$.

::: {.callout-note title="Open and closed intervals"}

::: {#def-open-closed-intervals} 
 
Let $a<b\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\cup\{-\infty\}$.
Here and throughout, inequalities involving $\pm\infty$ use the usual order on the extended real line.
We define the **open interval** $(a,b)$ as the subset of $\mathbb{R}$ given by
$$
(a,b):= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a< x < b \}.
$$ {#eq-open-interval}
If either $a=-\infty$ or $b=+\infty$, the interval is said to be **unbounded**.

When $a\neq-\infty$ and $b\neq+\infty$, we define the closed interval $[a,b]$ as
$$
[a,b]:= \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x \leq b \}.
$$

Intuitively speaking, the interval $(a,b)$ is _open_ because its boundary points **are not** part of it, while $[a,b]$ is _closed_ because its boundary points **are** part of it.

:::

:::

Not all intervals are either open or closed. For instance, when $a\neq-\infty$, we can define the interval $[a,b)$ as
$$
[a,b) := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a\leq x < b\},
$$
while, when $b\neq+\infty$, we can define the interval $(a,b]$ as
$$
(a,b] := \{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad a < x \leq b\}, 
$$
and it's clear that these interval are neither open nor closed in the sense of @def-open-closed-intervals




In the following, it will be useful to also consider the **symmetric open interval**
$$
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}\equiv(x_{0}-\varepsilon, x_{0}+\varepsilon)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\quad x_{0}-\varepsilon < x < x_{0} + \varepsilon\}
$$
centered at $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$ with length $2\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. It is not hard to see that if $x\in I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}$, then either $x-x_{0}< \varepsilon$  or $x_{0} - x <\varepsilon$. It then follows that $|x-x_{0}|<\varepsilon$, so that
$$ 
I_{x_{0},\varepsilon}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,| \quad d(x_{0},x)<\varepsilon\}. 
$$
Therefore, the symmetric open intervals of $\mathbb{R}$ may be determined through the distance function.



::: {.callout-note title="Accumulation point"}

::: {#def-accumulation-point}

A point $x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a **left accumulation point** for the subset $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x_0-r<x<x_0.
$$
A point $x_{0}\in \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a **right accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x_0<x<x_0+r.
$$

A point which is a left (right) accumulation point but not a right (left) accumulation point is called a **strict left accumulation point** (**strict right accumulation point**). 

A point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}$ is said to be an **accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $r>0$ there exists $x\in D$ with $x\neq x_0$ such that
$$
|x-x_0|<r,
$$ 
which means it is both a left and right accumulation point.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Isolated point"}

::: {#def-isolated-point}

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $x_{0}\in D$.
We say that $x_{0}$ is an **isolated point** of $D$ if there exists $r>0$ such that
$$
D\cap(x_{0}-r,x_{0}+r)=\{x_{0}\}.
$$

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Accumulation at infinity"}

::: {#def-accumulation-point-at-infinity}

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$.
We say that $+\infty$ is a **right accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $R>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x>R.
$$
We say that $-\infty$ is a **left accumulation point** for $D$ if for every $R>0$ there exists $x\in D$ such that
$$
x<-R.
$$

:::

:::
